intro: This last unit looks back and then looks forward. First it follows the Watchers story after it was written. You will read how later readers received it, in their own words: Jubilees and the Dead Sea Scrolls, Josephus and Philo, Justin Martyr, Tertullian and Augustine, the targums and Genesis Rabbah, and the Ethiopian church that kept 1 Enoch whole. Then you will use those texts to check modern claims, such as ancient astronauts or giants building the pyramids.

Then the unit turns to you. In the capstone you choose one hard question from this course and gather the primary documents: the Hebrew Bible, the Septuagint, 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Scrolls, the New Testament, the church fathers and the rabbis. You state at least two researchers' readings fairly. You weigh the evidence and write a calm argument, citing every text by book, chapter, verse and translation.

By the end you will be able to check a claim against the ancient texts and against a scholar's own words. You will be able to explain a disputed passage fairly and to disagree with respect. These skills reach well beyond this course. They help with any text, any scholar and any viral video.
bigQuestion: How have readers received the Watchers story over the centuries, and how can you argue fairly from the texts with readers who see them differently?

timeline.t: The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36) is written
Jubilees retells Genesis, with the Watchers sent to teach before they fall
Josephus, in Antiquities 1, compares the angels' sons to Greek giants
Justin Martyr's Second Apology links the angels' children with demons
Tertullian defends reading the Book of Enoch
Julius Africanus reads the sons of God as the line of Seth
Augustine, City of God 15.23, makes the Sethite view the leading Western reading
Genesis Rabbah records the view that the sons of God were sons of judges
James Bruce brings Ge'ez copies of 1 Enoch from Ethiopia to Europe
R. H. Charles's translation of 1 Enoch reaches many English readers
J. T. Milik publishes the Aramaic Enoch fragments from Qumran
Annette Yoshiko Reed publishes Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity

words.d: the study of how a text was read, retold and used by later readers over time
early Christian writers, roughly the 100s to 700s CE, whose works shaped later teaching
the reading that the sons of God in Genesis 6 were the godly descendants of Seth
the reading, found in rabbinic sources, that the sons of God were judges, nobles or rulers
an Aramaic translation of Scripture, often with added explanation, read in synagogues
the classical language of Ethiopia, in which 1 Enoch survives complete
the claim that visitors from space, remembered as gods, shaped early human history
the original text or object being studied, such as Genesis or a clay tablet
comparing manuscripts and translations to find the most likely original wording of a text
a one-sentence answer to a research question, which a paper defends with evidence
the strongest case against your thesis, which your paper states and answers fairly
presenting someone's view at its strongest before weighing it

test.q: In Jubilees 4, why are the Watchers first sent to earth?
choices: To teach people and do justice
test.why: Jubilees 4:15 says they came to teach and to do justice; they sin later.

test.q: What did Justin Martyr, in Second Apology 5, say the angels' children were?
test.why: Justin says the angels' children are those called demons.

test.q: Which writer defended the Book of Enoch in On the Apparel of Women?
test.why: Tertullian argued, around 200 CE, that Christians should not reject Enoch's book.

test.q: Which reading of the sons of God did Augustine teach in City of God 15.23?
How does Targum Onqelos render sons of God in Genesis 6:2?
test.why: Onqelos reads sons of the great ones, pointing to powerful men.

test.q: Which church keeps 1 Enoch in its canon?
test.why: 1 Enoch is canonical in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

test.q: What does Annette Yoshiko Reed (2005) argue about the Watchers story?
choices: It was invented in the Middle Ages
Jews and Christians each took it up and set it aside at different times
test.why: Reed argues against a simple Jewish-versus-Christian account of the story's fate.

test.q: Which fact best answers the claim that the Bible says giants built the pyramids?
choices: The KJV uses the word giants
No ancient text links giants to the pyramids, and the Bible sets its giants in and near Canaan
test.why: Numbers and Deuteronomy place tall peoples in and near Canaan; no text mentions pyramids.

test.q: Which witness reads sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8?
test.why: 4QDeut-j reads sons of God; the Masoretic Text and the KJV read sons (children) of Israel.

test.q: Which statement about Jude 14–15 is accurate?
test.why: Jude presents a prophecy of Enoch that closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9.

test.q: Which is a primary source for a paper on 1 Peter 3:19?
test.why: The passage itself is the primary source; everything written about it is secondary.

choices: The strongest case against your thesis, stated and answered fairly
test.why: A strong paper states the best case against its thesis and answers it fairly.

test.q: Which translation may be quoted word for word in this course?
choices: A modern scholar's translation in a 2015 book
test.why: The KJV is in the public domain. Modern translations and scholars' books are under copyright.

test.q: What does weighing the evidence decide in a capstone?
choices: Which reading best explains a text
test.why: Weighing judges which reading best explains the text, not what anyone should believe.

test.q: A classmate disagrees during your presentation. What is the best response?
choices: Thank them and ask which text or witness they would weigh differently
test.why: Turning to the evidence keeps the disagreement calm, respectful and useful.

write.prompt: Choose one question: Who are the sons of God in Genesis 6? Is 1 Peter 3:19 about the Watchers? Cite two or three primary documents (for example Genesis 6:1–4, 1 Enoch 6:1–6, Jude 14–15, Augustine, City of God 15.23). Explain what each says, state two researchers' readings fairly, and weigh them.
tips: Name every text by book, chapter, verse and translation, such as Genesis 6:4, King James Version (1611).
Attribute every view: 1 Enoch tells, Augustine read, Genesis Rabbah records, Reed argues.
State each researcher's reading at its strongest before you weigh it.
Paraphrase modern scholars in your own words and give the book and year; never quote their books.
Let your conclusion be as firm as the evidence, and no firmer.
